newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Ruch sale snag may deter investors - minister.
newsitem.headline: Polish Ruch sale snag may deter investors - minister.

text.p: Foreign firms may be deterred from investing in Poland if the planned sale of the newsstand chain Ruch SA to French Hachette Distribution Services is annulled, the economy minister said on Friday.

"I am afraid that if previous agreements (on the Ruch sale) are not implemented, this would have a negative impact on other planned privatisations and foreign capital interest in them," Wieslaw Kaczmarek told a news briefing.

The Polish treasury ministry, which has tentatively agreed to sell Ruch to a consortium of Polish firms led by Hachette, has recently said it might annul the deal if an offer made by a domestic bidder proves better.

Deputy treasury minister Leszek Juchniewicz said this week in an interview for the daily Gazeta Wyborcza that he might ask the minister to annul the tender and sign an agreement with a Polish consortium, Polska Grupa Kapitalowa, which includes trader Universal.
The minister's statement provoked protests from the Polish partners of Hachette's consortium, which said it contradicted the accord under which the group had the right of sole bidder for Ruch.

Universal spokeswoman Agnieszka Szostek has said her firm received a letter from the ministry asking the consortium, which includes Optimus, cable television operator Polsat and mineral water maker Multico, to make a final offer, which it would likely submit on Friday.
Szostek said on Friday that she did not know if the group had submitted the final offer to the ministry. No ministry official was available for comment on the issue.
Last month Juchniewicz told a news conference that the ministry was seeking better terms for the deal with Hachette.
Juchniewicz said the ministry's December acceptance of a price offer of a consortium of Polish firms led by Hachette embraced only frame terms of the sale and details still needed to be hammered out.

He said he expected Hachette to spend more and sooner on increasing Ruch's capital and strongly criticised Hachette for unveiling in French and then in Polish newspapers its price offer for Ruch before a final agreement was reached.

The daily Nowa Europa last month quoted Hachette's president Jean-Louis Nachury as saying his company would pay $84 million for a 75 percent stake in Ruch and then earmark a further $45 million for increasing its capital.
Ruch has a 65 percent share of Poland's press distribution market and owns 17,000 newsstands nationwide.
Its net profit in 1995 was 16.2 million zlotys on sales of 2.7 billion zlotys.
